132	## The Diagnostics tab
133	
134	`internal/netcheck` runs a pipeline against a target: resolve, route, reach,
135	connect, TLS, HTTP — one stage per step, chained so the UI can name exactly
136	which question is currently being asked. Earlier versions exposed a set of
137	checkboxes letting the user pick which tools to run; those are gone, because
138	which checks make sense follows automatically from the target and from
139	whatever has already failed.
140	
141	### One configurable timeout instead of five
142	
143	The pipeline used to hardcode five different per-stage timeouts (5s for DNS
144	and the initial dial, 8s for TLS and HTTP, 4s for ping) — a set of values
145	that was never really justified, just five separate guesses. A single
146	`check_timeout` setting replaces all five, defaulting to the old maximum so
147	nothing that used to succeed starts failing. The cost is explicit rather
148	than hidden: an unreachable host now spends up to 8 seconds on a DNS lookup
149	instead of 5, but the staged progress display makes that legible as "still
150	waiting on DNS" instead of an unexplained pause.
151	
152	Two values stay hardcoded rather than becoming settings, each for a reason
153	tied to what the check is *for*:
154	
155	- **`MinVersion: TLS 1.0`** in the handshake — the point of this probe is to
156	  detect an old TLS version, so making it configurable would let the tool
157	  become blind to exactly the thing it exists to report.
158	- **`InsecureSkipVerify`** — the TLS stage verifies the certificate chain
159	  itself, in order to say specifically *which* part of the chain failed. A
160	  single pass/fail from the Go standard library would collapse four
161	  distinguishable failure modes into one opaque error string.
162

165	Reachability failures usually look the same from the outside — no ping
166	reply, no TCP connect — regardless of cause. The route stage answers a

171	interface itself ("traffic leaves through the VPN adapter") rather than a
172	gateway IP address, because that's the form of the answer a person
173	recognizes without a second lookup.

175	This is implemented on top of `github.com/libp2p/go-netroute`, which
176	abstracts over three completely different underlying mechanisms — a
177	Windows API call, a Linux netlink query, and a BSD routing socket — behind

185	  is open.
186	- A lookup that fails is reported as *unknown*, never as *no route exists*

132	## The Diagnostics tab
133	
134	`internal/netcheck` runs a pipeline against a target: resolve, route, reach,
135	connect, TLS, HTTP — one stage per step, chained so the UI can name exactly
136	which question is currently being asked. Earlier versions exposed a set of
137	checkboxes letting the user pick which tools to run; those are gone, because
138	which checks make sense follows automatically from the target and from
139	whatever has already failed.
140	
141	### One configurable timeout instead of five
142	
143	The pipeline used to hardcode five different per-stage timeouts (5s for DNS
144	and the initial dial, 8s for TLS and HTTP, 4s for ping) — a set of values
145	that was never really justified, just five separate guesses. A single
146	`check_timeout` setting replaces all five, defaulting to the old maximum so
147	nothing that used to succeed starts failing. The cost is explicit rather
148	than hidden: an unreachable host now spends up to 8 seconds on a DNS lookup
149	instead of 5, but the staged progress display makes that legible as "still
150	waiting on DNS" instead of an unexplained pause.
151	
152	Two values stay hardcoded rather than becoming settings, each for a reason
153	tied to what the check is *for*:
154	
155	- **`MinVersion: TLS 1.0`** in the handshake — the point of this probe is to
156	  detect an old TLS version, so making it configurable would let the tool
157	  become blind to exactly the thing it exists to report.
158	- **`InsecureSkipVerify`** — the TLS stage verifies the certificate chain
159	  itself, in order to say specifically *which* part of the chain failed. A
160	  single pass/fail from the Go standard library would collapse four
161	  distinguishable failure modes into one opaque error string.
162	
163	### The route stage
164	
165	Reachability failures usually look the same from the outside — no ping
166	reply, no TCP connect — regardless of cause. The route stage answers a
167	question none of the other checks can: *which interface will traffic
168	actually leave through?* When a VPN has captured the default route, a host
169	that's reachable from elsewhere becomes unreachable locally, and every other
170	check reports only the symptom. The route stage's summary names the
171	interface itself ("traffic leaves through the VPN adapter") rather than a
172	gateway IP address, because that's the form of the answer a person
173	recognizes without a second lookup.
174	
175	This is implemented on top of `github.com/libp2p/go-netroute`, which
176	abstracts over three completely different underlying mechanisms — a
177	Windows API call, a Linux netlink query, and a BSD routing socket — behind
178	one interface, needs no elevated privileges, and resolves a route in about
179	2 milliseconds.
180	
181	A few points shape how the route stage behaves:
182	
183	- It never blocks anything else. A machine whose routing table can't be
184	  read still has a perfectly answerable question about whether a given port
185	  is open.
186	- A lookup that fails is reported as *unknown*, never as *no route exists*
187	  — those are different facts, and conflating them would misreport a local

  — those are different facts, and conflating them would misreport a local
  permissions or platform quirk as "this host is unreachable."

  to describe an address some other check in the same run actually touched

186	- A lookup that fails is reported as *unknown*, never as *no route exists*
187	  — those are different facts, and conflating them would misreport a local
188	  permissions or platform quirk as "this host is unreachable."
189	- If one address family (typically IPv6) has no route while the other does,
190	  that's reported as a warning with a count — worth surfacing, since a
191	  client that prefers IPv6 will hang before it falls back to IPv4.
192	- It reuses the addresses the `resolve` stage already found rather than
193	  resolving the target a second time, so the route it reports is guaranteed
194	  to describe an address some other check in the same run actually touched
195	  (important for round-robin DNS names, where two independent lookups can
196	  return different addresses).

**Files.** `trace_form.go` holds what the form does: `traceable()` (the one
availability, read by the button, the header and the handler, Rule 130),
`traceFromForm()` (the `enter` handler), the target validation and
`traceUnusedNotice`. `trace_level.go` holds the sub-level: `startFromForm`,
`handleKeyTrace`, `escFromTrace` (with `restoreFormFocus`), `traceTitle` and
`traceShortcuts`.

**Order of refusals in `traceFromForm`.** An unsupported platform
(`launchable()`, macOS, Windows, WSL1) comes first: the button is greyed and
the reason is in the footer. Then a trace already running (`reasonTraceBusy`).
Then the target.

**Target validation (Rule 140).** The target goes through `parsePathTarget`,
the parser of the Path tab, so an empty, invalid, `host:port` or IPv6 value
gets the same sentence as on the Path tab (first letter capitalized). The
failure is carried twice: the Target field is underlined
(`traceMarks`, `InvalidMarks.Sync`, from `Update()` only) and the error sits
in the footer at level Error, derived from `traceValidation.Status()` in
`statusLine()`. Nothing is invalid before the first refused `enter` on the
button; after that, every edit of the Target revalidates (`revalidateTrace`).
`enter` on a text field still runs the diagnostics and does not validate
the trace target.

**Port and DNS Server.** The trace probes the path to a host, so both fields
are ignored. When either holds a non-blank value, `traceUnusedNotice` posts an
Info notice on the Path model's footer (`Port is not used by the path trace`,
`DNS Server is not used by the path trace`, or both). It is posted after
`startFromForm`, because launching clears that footer. The values stay in the
form.

**Coupling with the Path tab.** The sub-level has no model of its own: it
drives `m.pathModel`. Starting from the form therefore overwrites the Path
tab's field (`prefill`) and its previous run, and the trace shows on both: the
Path tab sees the same hops, and `esc` there cancels the same run. Going back
to the form does not clear the Path model. This coupling disappears when the
Path tab is removed (P2-02).

input.new_string:
every other key is dropped by `handleKeyTrace` and never reaches
`PathModel.handleKey`, whose `handleDoneError` would make its hidden field
live again. No `enter`, `ctrl+r` or `ctrl+o` here: to trace again, go back to
the form. `tab` and `shift+tab` still switch tabs (the router handles them
before the state), so the sub-level survives a visit to another tab.

**Files.** `trace_form.go` holds what the form does: `traceable()` (the one
availability, read by the button, the header and the handler, Rule 130),
`traceFromForm()` (the `enter` handler), the target validation and
`traceUnusedNotice`. `trace_level.go` holds the sub-level: `startFromForm`,
`handleKeyTrace`, `escFromTrace` (with `restoreFormFocus`), `traceTitle` and
`traceShortcuts`.

**Order of refusals in `traceFromForm`.** An unsupported platform
(`launchable()`, macOS, Windows, WSL1) comes first: the button is greyed and
the reason is in the footer. Then a trace already running (`reasonTraceBusy`).
Then the target.

**Target validation (Rule 140).** The target goes through `parsePathTarget`,
the parser of the Path tab, so an empty, invalid, `host:port` or IPv6 value
gets the same sentence as on the Path tab (first letter capitalized). The
failure is carried twice: the Target field is underlined
(`traceMarks`, `InvalidMarks.Sync`, from `Update()` only) and the error sits
in the footer at level Error, derived from `traceValidation.Status()` in
`statusLine()`. Nothing is invalid before the first refused `enter` on the
button; after that, every edit of the Target revalidates (`revalidateTrace`).
`enter` on a text field still runs the diagnostics and does not validate
the trace target.

**Port and DNS Server.** The trace probes the path to a host, so both fields
are ignored. When either holds a non-blank value, `traceUnusedNotice` posts an
Info notice on the Path model's footer (`Port is not used by the path trace`,
`DNS Server is not used by the path trace`, or both). It is posted after
`startFromForm`, because launching clears that footer. The values stay in the
form.

**Coupling with the Path tab.** The sub-level has no model of its own: it
drives `m.pathModel`. Starting from the form therefore overwrites the Path
tab's field (`prefill`) and its previous run, and the trace shows on both: the
Path tab sees the same hops, and `esc` there cancels the same run. Going back
to the form does not clear the Path model. This coupling disappears when the
Path tab is removed (P2-02).

# Keybindings

DevDesk's keyboard vocabulary has one rule at its core: **no bare letter is
navigation.** Arrow keys and `Tab`/`Shift+Tab` navigate; a lowercase letter
is always a local filter or toggle, an uppercase letter is always a
resource action, and there are no vim-style `hjkl` aliases.

## Navigation

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `↑` / `↓` | Move up/down in a list or table |
| `PageUp` / `PageDown` | Scroll by page |
| `Home` / `End` | Go to top / bottom |
| `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` | Move between breadcrumb tabs |
| `←` | Go back to the parent level (drill up) |
| `→` | Enter the selected group/directory (drill down) |
| `Enter` | Select / confirm (in selection mode) |
| `Esc` | Go back to the parent level, or cancel/close a modal |

## Resource actions — uppercase, same meaning everywhere

| Key | Action | Key | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| `N` | Create | `E` | Edit |
| `D` | Delete | `M` | Rename (*mv*) |
| `S` | Scan | `A` | Scan all |
| `F` | Sync / refresh (*fetch*) | `C` | Clone selector |
| `T` | Terminal | `O` | Open in IDE |
| `W` | Open in browser | `L` | Logs |
| `V` | Pager | `K` | Stop / kill |
| `P` | Prune | `B` | Registry browser |
| `G` | Pull (*get*) | `U` | Login / logout |
| `X` | Exclude | `R` | MR · PR |
| `I` | Issues | `Y` | Copy (path, content, MCP connect command) |
| `H` | Open network diagnostics on this target; in Network Diagnostics, trace the path to it | `J` | Jump to the related resource — a container's image, in the OCI view |

`Q` and `Z` are the only free letters left.

Three declared exceptions to "uppercase for actions": `o` (open the resolved
CI pipeline, security/results/CI tab only), `ctrl+y` (copy the `docker run`
command, OCI launch form) and `ctrl+o` (write a fix to disk, security
results) — narrow enough that reserving a global uppercase for any of them
would cost more than it buys. `ctrl+o` is the one binding that changes a
file, so it always opens a confirmation that defaults to No.

## Security results — Remediation and fixes

| Key | Where | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `S` | Remediation tab | Scan the candidate base images |
| `space` | Remediation tab | Choose the candidate under the cursor for its stage |
| `enter` | Remediation tab | Open the diff in the viewer |
| `ctrl+o` | Remediation tab | Write the chosen base images into the Dockerfiles |
| `ctrl+o` | Misconfigurations tab | Write the built-in fix for the selected finding, then re-scan to verify it |

See [Remediation](../explanation/scanning.md#remediation).

## Network Diagnostics — Forward tab

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `N` | Open a new forward — a TCP redirection, or a named HTTP route |
| `space` | Pause the selected forward, or resume a paused or unbound one |
| `K` | Delete the selected forward, after a confirmation |
| `←` / `→` | Change the `Type` field (`TCP` / `HTTP`) in the form |
| `/` | Search by port or target |
| `.` | Cycle the sort column |

`space` is Pause/Resume — a control, not a new capital — and `K` greys out
when there is nothing selected to delete.

## Network Diagnostics — Path tab

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `enter` | Trace the path to the host typed in the target field, or trace again once a trace is done |
| `esc` | While a trace runs: cancel it and keep the hops already seen. Once it is done: edit the target again (the value is kept) |
| `↑` `↓` `PageUp` `PageDown` `Home` `End` | Move in the hop table |
| `Tab` | Switch tab |

The field takes a host name or an IPv4 address, with no port: `host:80` is
refused (`Path ignores ports: enter a host or IP address only`). Nothing is
sent until you press `enter`. `enter` is greyed out on a platform that cannot trace (the trace runs on Linux
only, for now).

From the Diagnostics tab, `H` on the **Local route** row of the results opens
the Path tab with that target's host already in the field. It does not start a
trace; press `enter` there. On any other row `H` is greyed out. If a trace is
already running, `H` only switches to the Path tab.

## Lowercase — local filters and toggles, view by view

Lowercase letters never modify anything; they're local and can repeat
across views. Examples: `r`/`p`/`s`/`t`/`z` in Containers are cumulative
state filters; `c`/`h`/`m`/`l` in Security are cumulative severity filters;
`t`/`u`/`l`/`e`/`n`/`z` in Network Diagnostics filter protocol/state (Ports tab); `g` in
Workspaces opens fuzzy-find navigation (jump to any directory under the
workspaces root by typing part of its path), the same letter the document
viewer uses for its own, unrelated "go to line" prompt. Each view declares
its own set — see `internal/ui/keymap` for the full, per-view list.

## Global

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `ctrl+p` | Open the command palette — from anywhere, including inside a focused field |
| `:` | Open the command palette too, except while editing a text field |
| `/` | Search / filter |
| `?` | Open help |
| `q` | Quit view/app |
| `ctrl+r` | Refresh — nothing else |

Only three `Ctrl` combinations exist in the whole app: `ctrl+c` (SIGINT),
`ctrl+r` (refresh), `ctrl+p` (command palette). Most other `Ctrl` letters are
already claimed by the terminal, `screen`, or `tmux` (`ctrl+a`, `ctrl+b`,
flow control on `ctrl+s`/`ctrl+q`, and `ctrl+i`/`m`/`j`/`h` are literally
Tab/Enter/LF/Backspace), so a fourth would be reclaiming ground `Shift`
already gives for free.

## Forms

| Key | Role |
|---|---|
| `↑` / `↓` | Move between fields |
| `←` / `→` | Cycle a closed-set field's value |
| `Space` | Toggle a checkbox |
| `Enter` | Confirm the focused button / action |
| `Esc` | Cancel / close |

`Tab`/`Shift+Tab` is reserved for switching tabs and never moves focus
between form fields.

## Document viewer

Opened from another view (a file in Workspaces, a log in Containers);
`Esc` returns to where it was opened from.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `f` | Toggle the document's derived view (tree for JSON/XML, rendered form for Markdown) |
| `c` | Syntax coloring on/off |
| `w` | Soft wrap |
| `v` | Cycle the minimum log level shown (logs only) |
| `/` | Search — filters **and** highlights matches |
| `s` | Case-sensitive search toggle |
| `n` | Line numbers, from the document's own numbering |
| `g` | Go to a line (prompts for a number) |
| `ctrl+r` / `F` | Reload once / follow (tail) |
| `V` | Open in the system pager (container logs only) |
| `Y` | Copy the document's content to the clipboard |
| `O` | Open the file in the configured IDE (files only) |
